html:
Lothal is an excavated town of the Indus Valley civilisation in Gujarat, western India, near the head of the Gulf of Khambhat. It was built from about 2300 BCE and is one of the southernmost Harappan sites.

Its best-known feature is a large brick-lined basin, about 220 metres long, on the east side of the town. The archaeologist S. R. Rao, who dug the site from 1955, read it as a dock that boats entered from an old river channel at high tide. Others have argued it was a water tank for drinking or irrigation; the dock reading is still the most common.

The town had a raised citadel, a warehouse, streets of houses with baths and drains, and workshops.

  • Bead makers worked carnelian and agate, prized in Mesopotamia.
  • Copper smiths and shell workers made tools and bangles.
  • A Persian Gulf type seal points to sea trade with Dilmun.

Lothal fits the picture of Indus goods reaching Mesopotamia by sea, the Meluhha trade with Sumer. Like Dholavira to the north, it was slowly abandoned as the Indus cities declined after about 1900 BCE.
sum: Lothal is an excavated town of the Indus Valley civilisation in Gujarat, western India, near the head of the Gulf of Khambhat. It was built from about 2300 BCE and is one of the southernmost Harappan sites.
